candidate.answerReason: Every integer n from 2 through 59 has a prime divisor r at most 59. That divisor also divides P, so it is a proper divisor of P+n. Every term is composite.

methods.label: Find a divisor of every term
methods.explanation:
The useful feature of \(P\) is that it contains every prime that could divide any of the integers \(2,3,\ldots,59\).

Take any integer \(n\) in this range, and let \(r\) be its smallest positive divisor greater than \(1\). This divisor must be prime: if \(r\) were composite, a factor strictly between \(1\) and \(r\) would also divide \(n\), contradicting the choice of \(r\).

Since \(r\le n\le59\), the prime \(r\) is a factor of \(P\). Write \(P=ru\) and \(n=rv\), where \(u\) and \(v\) are positive integers. Then
\[
P+n=r(u+v).
\]
Both factors exceed \(1\), because \(r\ge2\) and \(u+v\ge2\). Thus \(P+n\) is composite. This argument applies to all \(58\) terms, so \(\boxed{N=0}\), choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
methods.levelReason: The proof uses only factors, prime and composite numbers, and factoring a sum with a common integer factor.

candidate.annotationRationale: The task is to establish compositeness uniformly across the sequence. The method constructs one proper divisor for every term and explains why a prime divisor exists. Complete prime factorizations, uniqueness, and prime-exponent calculations are not used, so the broader prime-factorization node is unnecessary.
